intro: Paderewski records the F♯-major Nocturne in New York in May 1917. His piano belongs to an age of rolled chords and hands that can speak at different moments.

sections.label: A · The slow F♯-major song
sections.mNote: A decorated right-hand melody above bass notes and chords

sections.label: B · A dotted tune runs faster
sections.mNote: Doppio movimento begins sotto voce over a C♯ bass

sections.label: A′ · The slow song returns
sections.mNote: The opening tempo and melody return after a pause

cues.title: A melody with elbows
cues.text: Chopin’s melody curls through quick ornaments while the left hand places bass notes and chords beneath it. Paderewski’s playing often separates the hands’ attacks and spreads chords, giving the tune room to lean ahead of its accompaniment or linger behind.
cues.evidence: Opening piano writing: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 1–16, https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86. Jonathan Woolf discusses hand dislocation and arpeggiated chords across Paderewski’s Victor recordings: https://www.musicweb-international.com/classrev/2017/May/Paderewski_American_7505.htm

cues.title: New York, May 1917
cues.text: On 14 May 1917 Paderewski plays this nocturne for Victor in New York. The company issues the first take. A few weeks later he returns to record Chopin’s G♭-major Butterfly Étude.
cues.evidence: APR 7505 session listing: Nocturne, matrix C 19781-1, 14 May 1917; Étude Op. 25 No. 9, 18 June 1917. https://www.musicweb-international.com/classrev/2017/May/Paderewski_American_7505.htm

cues.title: Quickened, still under the breath
cues.text: The central passage starts sotto voce, its dotted tune threaded through quick accompanying notes. Chopin asks for twice the motion. The left hand’s leaps and the insistent dotted patterns gradually turn the murmur into a struggle.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 25–40; Mieczysław Tomaszewski discusses the dotted rhythms and central climax. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86; https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The opening turn returns
cues.text: The repeated figures lose speed and sink lower. A pause, then A♯ rises to B: the little turn that begins the nocturne. The returning song keeps its old outline while Chopin fits new ornaments into it.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 47–52. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: “What is lost is lost”
cues.text: In his 1909 essay on rubato, Paderewski laughs at the rule that time borrowed from one phrase must be paid back in another. “What is lost is lost,” he writes. “For any lawlessness there is, after a certain term, proscription.”
cues.evidence: Ignacy Jan Paderewski, ‘Tempo Rubato’, in Henry T. Finck, Success in Music and How It Is Won (1909), chapter 28, pp. 454–461; reprinted by the USC Polish Music Center: https://polishmusic.usc.edu/research/publications/polish-music-journal/vol4no1/paderewski-tempo-rubato/

transitions.title: The bass turns to C♯
transitions.to: B · A dotted tune runs faster
transitions.how: The slow section lingers on repeated A♯s. A C♯ bass starts the middle, supporting a dominant seventh with E♯, G♯ and B. Doppio movimento doubles the motion, and the right hand divides its work between a dotted tune and quick notes underneath. The opening of the passage is marked sotto voce.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 24–26. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86

transitions.title: The quick figures die away
transitions.from: B · A dotted tune runs faster
transitions.how: Chopin writes molto rallentando, smorzando over repeated figures above a low C♯. The left hand then falls silent. After a pause, A♯ and B introduce the opening tune at its first tempo; the bass moves from C♯ to F♯ beneath the restored melody.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 47–50. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
